topic: Etymology of Secretary
questionText: The English word 'Secretary' is derived from the Latin word 'Secretarius', which originally denoted:

options.text: A military commander of provincial garrisons
A confidential officer or keeper of secrets entrusted with private matters
A maritime customs collector at Roman ports
A public auctioneer of agricultural estates

explanation: Derived from Latin 'Secretum' / 'Secretarius', a Secretary historically signified a trusted person handling confidential correspondence and records (paralleled by Roman 'Scribae' and ancient Indian 'Amatya'/'Sachiva'/'Chitnis').
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Secretary

topic: Mandatory Qualification of Company Secretary
questionText: Under Section 2(24) of the Companies Act, 2013, an individual appointed as a Company Secretary of a Joint Stock Company MUST be a member of which statutory institute?

options.text: The Bar Council of Maharashtra and Goa
The Indian Institute of Banking and Finance
The Institute of Company Secretaries of India (ICSI)
The Institute of Cost Accountants of India

explanation: Only an individual holding valid membership of the Institute of Company Secretaries of India (ICSI), New Delhi—constituted under the Company Secretaries Act, 1980—can be appointed as a Company Secretary.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Secretary

topic: Personal Secretary vs Institutional Secretary
questionText: Who appoints a 'Personal (Private) Secretary' such as an assistant to a busy surgeon, senior advocate, film actor, or Member of Parliament?

options.text: The Managing Committee of a Registered Co-operative Bank
The Registrar of Companies through form DIR-12
Shareholders voting by Poll at an Annual General Meeting
A busy individual professional or VIP to manage personal appointments, correspondence, and schedules

explanation: A Personal Secretary is appointed by busy executives or professionals to handle personal diary, correspondence, and visitors, requiring no statutory corporate membership.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Secretary

topic: Paid-up Capital Threshold for Whole-Time Company Secretary
questionText: Under the Companies Act, 2013 read with Companies (Appointment and Remuneration of Managerial Personnel) Rules, every listed company AND every other public/applicable company having paid-up share capital of how much or more must appoint a whole-time Company Secretary?

options.text: ₹10 crore or more
₹50 lakh or more
₹100 crore or more
₹1 lakh or more

explanation: Under Rule 8A / Section 203 rules as updated and taught in MSBSHSE Class 11 SP, every listed company and other companies having paid-up share capital of ₹10 crore or more must have a whole-time Company Secretary.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Secretary

topic: Secretary of Government Department
questionText: How is the 'Secretary of a Government Department' (such as the Finance Secretary or Commerce Secretary) appointed and whom does he/she advise?

options.text: Appointed by Rotary Clubs to record minutes of charity dinners
Appointed from senior civil services (typically IAS) to act as the administrative head of a ministry and advise the Minister on policy and execution
Selected exclusively from freshly enrolled law graduates with zero administrative experience
Elected directly by shareholders of private companies for a two-year rotation

explanation: A Secretary of a Government Department is a senior career civil servant (usually IAS) functioning as the executive/administrative head of a Ministry/Department under the political leadership of a Minister.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Secretary

topic: Secretary as 'Eyes, Ears, and Hands' of the Company
questionText: Why did Lord Denning in Panorama Developments (Guildford) Ltd. v. Fidelis Furnishing Fabrics Ltd. recognise the modern Company Secretary as a senior administrative officer with ostensible authority—rather than a mere clerk?

options.text: Because the Board of Directors is subordinate to the Personal Secretary
Because the Company Secretary personally owns at least 51% of the company's equity
Because the Company Secretary can amend the Companies Act unilaterally
Because the Company Secretary represents the company in administrative matters, signs administrative contracts, ensures statutory compliance, and links the Board, shareholders, and regulators

explanation: Modern jurisprudence recognises the Company Secretary as a Key Managerial Personnel (KMP) and Chief Compliance Officer who binds the company on administrative matters—far beyond mere clerical typing.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Secretary

topic: Statutory vs Non-Statutory Duties of Company Secretary
questionText: A newly appointed Company Secretary is reviewing her compliance calendar under Section 205 of the Companies Act, 2013. Which action falls squarely within her statutory duties—and what limitation restricts her authority?

options.text: Declaring interim dividend unilaterally and altering the Object Clause without shareholder approval
Dismissing the Managing Director and appointing statutory auditors on her own signature
Reporting to the Board about compliance with the Act/rules and facilitating Secretarial Audit, BUT she cannot borrow money in the company's name or allot shares without specific Board authorisation
Borrowing ₹50 crore via debentures without convening a Board Meeting

explanation: Under Section 205, a CS guides the Board on statutory compliance and governance, yet policy powers like borrowing funds, issuing/allotting shares, or making calls belong strictly to the Board of Directors unless duly authorised.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Secretary

topic: Comparing Institutional Secretaries Across Entities
questionText: Compare the governing statutes applicable to Institutional Secretaries of (i) a Sports & Cultural Club registered as a trust/society, (ii) a District Urban Co-operative Society in Pune, and (iii) a Public Limited Company:

options.text: (i) Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881; (ii) Sale of Goods Act, 1930; (iii) FEMA, 1999
(i) Societies Registration Act, 1860 / Public Trusts Act; (ii) Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960; (iii) Companies Act, 2013
All three are governed exclusively by the Indian Contract Act, 1872 without registration
(i) Companies Act, 2013; (ii) Indian Partnership Act, 1932; (iii) Reserve Bank Act, 1934

explanation: Non-profit associations operate under Societies Registration/Public Trusts laws, Maharashtra co-operatives follow the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960, and Joint Stock Companies are governed by the Companies Act, 2013.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Secretary

topic: One Person Company (OPC)
questionText: Introduced under Section 2(62) of the Companies Act, 2013, how many members does a 'One Person Company (OPC)' have, and what safeguard ensures continuity upon that member's death?

options.text: Only 1 corporate foreign body as sole member without any nominee
Minimum 2 members and maximum 200 members
Only 1 member, with mandatory nomination of a natural-person Nominee in the Memorandum of Association
Minimum 7 members with no nominee requirement

explanation: An OPC has a single member and must indicate in its MOA the name of a nominee (with prior written consent) who becomes the member in the event of the sole subscriber's death or incapacity.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Joint Stock Company

topic: Private vs Public Company Member Limits
questionText: Under Sections 2(68) and 2(71) of the Companies Act, 2013, what are the minimum and maximum member limits for a Private Company and a Public Company?

options.text: Private Company: min 2, max 200 (excluding present/past employee-members); Public Company: min 7, unlimited maximum
Private Company: min 7, max 50; Public Company: min 2, max 500
Private Company: min 1, max 100; Public Company: min 10, max 1,000
Both require min 5 and max 200 members

explanation: A Private Company requires at least 2 members and caps membership at 200 (excluding employees and former employees who acquired shares while employed), whereas a Public Company requires at least 7 members with no upper cap.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Joint Stock Company

topic: Section 8 Charitable Company
questionText: A company licensed under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013 to promote commerce, art, science, sports, education, or charity is strictly prohibited from doing which of the following?

options.text: Employing salaried teachers or researchers
Holding an Annual General Meeting
Opening a bank account in India
Paying any dividend to its members (all profits must be applied solely toward promoting its objects)

explanation: Section 8 non-profit companies enjoy exemption from adding 'Limited'/'Private Limited' to their names, must apply surpluses solely to their charitable/educational objects, and cannot distribute dividends to members.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Joint Stock Company

topic: Separate Legal Entity — Salomon Principle
questionText: What landmark corporate-law principle was established in 'Salomon v. Salomon & Co. Ltd.'?

options.text: Creditors can seize private jewellery of minority shareholders at will
Shareholders are personally liable for 100% of corporate debentures even in a company limited by shares
A company ceases to exist on the day its founder retires
Upon incorporation, a company becomes a distinct legal person entirely separate from its subscribers/shareholders, even if one shareholder holds virtually all shares

explanation: Incorporation creates a veil of separate corporate personality: the company's assets, debts, and contracts belong to the company itself, not to its shareholders personally.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Joint Stock Company

topic: Holding, Subsidiary, and Associate Company Thresholds
questionText: Company P acquires 56% of the total voting power of Company Q and 24% of the total voting power of Company R (without controlling R's Board composition). Under the Companies Act, 2013, how are Q and R related to P?

options.text: Company Q is a Subsidiary Company of P [Sec 2(87)], and Company R is an Associate Company of P [Sec 2(6)]
Both Q and R are wholly-owned Subsidiary Companies of P
Company Q is an Associate Company and Company R is a Dormant Company
Neither Q nor R has any statutory relationship with P unless holding reaches 75%

explanation: Holding >50% of total voting power (or controlling Board composition) creates a Holding–Subsidiary relationship [Sec 2(87)], whereas 'significant influence' (≥20% up to 50% voting power) creates an Associate Company [Sec 2(6)].
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Joint Stock Company

topic: Dormant Company under Section 455
questionText: When can a registered company apply to the Registrar for 'Dormant Company' status under Section 455 of the Companies Act, 2013?

options.text: Only after being wound up and struck off by NCLT
When formed for a future project or to hold an asset/intellectual property and having no 'significant accounting transactions', or remaining inactive for the last two financial years
When it employs more than 5,000 factory workers
Whenever it earns record export profits for three consecutive years

explanation: Section 455 allows an inactive company (no significant accounting transactions / not filing financial statements & annual returns for 2 years, or incorporated to hold IP/land for a future project) to obtain Dormant status with lower compliance costs.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Joint Stock Company

topic: Counting the 200-Member Ceiling in a Private Company
questionText: Deccan Precision Pvt. Ltd. currently has: 175 individual outside shareholders, 18 joint-holdings (36 individuals holding shares in 18 pairs), 22 current employees holding ESOP shares, and 12 retired employees who were allotted shares while in employment. Under Section 2(68), what is the statutory member count against the 200-member limit?

options.text: 175 members — because joint-holders are excluded completely
245 members — violating the 200-member limit and triggering forced conversion
193 members — well within the 200-member statutory ceiling
227 members — because retired employees are counted

explanation: Under Section 2(68): (a) joint holders of shares are counted as ONE single member (18 pairs = 18); (b) current employee-members (22) and former employees who became members during employment (12) are EXCLUDED. Statutory count = 175 + 18 = 193 ≤ 200.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Joint Stock Company

topic: Company Limited by Guarantee vs Limited by Shares
questionText: In a Company Limited by Guarantee having no share capital, when can members actually be called upon to pay the guaranteed amount stated in the Memorandum?

options.text: Only in the event of winding up of the company, toward payment of the company's debts/liabilities and costs of winding up
At every quarterly Board Meeting to fund routine working capital
Within 30 days of incorporation under Section 10A
Whenever the company declares an interim dividend

explanation: In a company limited by guarantee, the guaranteed sum acts as 'reserve liability' enforceable solely upon liquidation/winding up if corporate assets prove inadequate—not as working capital during active life.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Joint Stock Company

topic: Three Stages in Formation of a Company
questionText: Under the Companies Act, 2013 as presented in the MSBSHSE syllabus, what are the three sequential stages in the formation of a company having share capital?

options.text: (1) Prospectus Audit, (2) Annual General Meeting, and (3) Promotion
(1) Promotion, (2) Incorporation of a Company, and (3) Commencement of Business
(1) Listing on NSE, (2) Promotion, and (3) Declaration of Dividend
(1) Winding Up, (2) Amalgamation, and (3) Incorporation

explanation: Company formation proceeds sequentially through Promotion (conceiving the business idea & assembling resources), Incorporation (registration with ROC/CRC), and Commencement of Business (Section 10A filing).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Formation of a Company

topic: Corporate Identity Number (CIN)
questionText: Upon issuing the Certificate of Incorporation, the Registrar / Central Registration Centre allots a unique Corporate Identity Number (CIN) consisting of how many alphanumeric characters?

options.text: 12-digit Aadhaar code
10-digit PAN code
8-digit DIN code
21-digit alphanumeric code

explanation: Every incorporated company in India receives a 21-character alphanumeric Corporate Identity Number (CIN) encoding listing status, industry code, state code, year of incorporation, ownership type, and registration number.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Formation of a Company

topic: Integrated Electronic Incorporation Form
questionText: Which integrated web-based electronic form on the MCA portal enables name reservation, company incorporation, DIN allotment, PAN, TAN, and EPFO/ESIC/GSTIN registration in a single workflow?

options.text: Form MGT-14
SPICe+ (Simplified Proforma for Incorporating Company Electronically Plus — INC-32)
Form MBP-1
Form SH-4

explanation: SPICe+ (INC-32) streamlines incorporation and allied statutory registrations through a single integrated MCA21 electronic interface.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Formation of a Company

topic: Fiduciary Position of Promoters
questionText: What is the exact legal relationship of a 'Promoter' [Section 2(69)] toward the company he is promoting?

options.text: A fully authorised agent whose pre-incorporation contracts automatically bind the unborn company
An independent speculator free to sell his personal land to the company at hidden mark-ups
A fiduciary relationship of utmost trust and good faith — neither strictly an agent nor a trustee (since the company is not yet in existence), forbidding secret profits
A statutory employee entitled to fix his own lifelong salary without disclosure

explanation: Because an unincorporated company does not legally exist yet, a promoter cannot be its strict agent or trustee, but stands in a fiduciary position requiring full disclosure of any personal interest or profit to an independent Board/prospectus.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Formation of a Company

topic: Commencement of Business Declaration (Section 10A)
questionText: Under Section 10A of the Companies Act, 2013, within how many days of incorporation must a company having share capital file a declaration by a director that every subscriber to the MOA has paid the value of shares agreed to be taken?

options.text: Within 180 days from the date of incorporation
Only after holding the fifth AGM
Within 15 days from incorporation
Within 3 years from incorporation

explanation: Under Section 10A, a company having share capital cannot commence business or exercise borrowing powers unless a director files a verified declaration within 180 days of incorporation confirming subscriber payment (plus registered office verification).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Formation of a Company

topic: Preliminary (Pre-Incorporation) Contracts
questionText: Before 'Konkan Agro Ltd.' is incorporated, its promoters sign a contract with a machinery vendor in the proposed company's name. After incorporation, how can Konkan Agro Ltd. legally make that contract enforceable between itself and the vendor?

options.text: By passing a simple Board resolution retrospectively ratifying the pre-incorporation signature
It binds the company automatically on the day CIN is generated without any action
By entering into a fresh contract ('Novation') with the vendor after incorporation, provided such contract is warranted by the terms of incorporation
Pre-incorporation contracts can never be adopted even by signing a fresh contract

explanation: Because the company was non-existent when signed, it cannot retrospectively 'ratify' a pre-incorporation contract under agency law; instead, novation (entering a new post-incorporation contract under Specific Relief Act Sections 15/19) binds the company and discharges promoters.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Formation of a Company

topic: Consequences of Failing Section 10A Compliance
questionText: Sahyadri BioTech Pvt. Ltd. was incorporated with share capital on 1st April 2025, but 200 days have elapsed without filing the Section 10A Commencement of Business declaration, and the Registrar has reasonable cause to believe it is not carrying on operations. What statutory consequence may follow?

options.text: Exemption from filing annual returns for the next five years
Forfeiture of the Registrar's own office
Automatic conversion of the company into a Statutory Corporation
Monetary penalties on the company and officers-in-default, AND the Registrar may initiate action to remove (strike off) the company's name from the Register of Companies

explanation: Under Section 10A(2) & (3), default attracts civil penalties AND if no declaration is filed within 180 days with no active operations, the ROC may initiate striking off under Section 248.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Formation of a Company

topic: Remedy for Promoter's Undisclosed Secret Profit
questionText: Promoter Kulkarni bought an industrial plot in his personal name for ₹80 lakh AFTER initiating promotion of a company, and then sold it to the newly formed company for ₹1.15 crore while concealing his personal ownership from the Board and Prospectus. Upon discovery, what remedies are available to the company?

options.text: All public shareholders must pay Kulkarni an additional 10% bonus
The company may rescind the contract (recovering ₹1.15 crore on returning the plot) OR retain the plot and compel Kulkarni to surrender the ₹35 lakh secret profit (or claim damages)
The company has no remedy once the Sale Deed is registered
Kulkarni is entitled to keep ₹35 lakh as automatic promoter brokerage

explanation: Breach of fiduciary duty through undisclosed profit entitles the company either to rescind the contract or affirm the asset purchase while recovering the ₹35 lakh secret profit.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Formation of a Company

topic: Decoding Information Embedded in a 21-Digit CIN
questionText: Inspect the sample CIN `L28920MH2018PLC305412`. What three facts can a Company Secretary immediately deduce from `L`, `MH`, and `PLC`?

options.text: `L` = Listed on a recognised stock exchange; `MH` = Registered in Maharashtra; `PLC` = Public Limited Company
`L` = Liquidated company; `MH` = Manufacturing Heavy; `PLC` = Private Liability Concern
`L` = Limited by Guarantee; `MH` = Ministry Holding; `PLC` = Partnership Limited Co.
`L` = Unlisted company; `MH` = Micro Holding; `PLC` = One Person Company

explanation: In a 21-digit CIN: position 1 (`L` = Listed, `U` = Unlisted), positions 2–6 = NIC industry code, positions 7–8 (`MH` = Maharashtra), positions 9–12 = year of incorporation, positions 13–15 (`PLC` = Public Limited, `PTC` = Private Limited, `OPC` = One Person Co., `GOI`/`SGC` = Govt Co.), positions 16–21 = ROC registration number.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Formation of a Company

Memorandum of Association (MOA)
Articles of Association (AOA)

options.text: Shipping Bill
Statement in Lieu of Prospectus
Letter of Credit
Articles of Association (AOA)

topic: Doctrine of Ultra Vires
questionText: Under the 'Doctrine of Ultra Vires' (established in Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co. Ltd. v. Riche), if directors apply corporate funds to an activity completely outside the Object Clause of the Memorandum of Association, what is the legal status of that act?

options.text: Wholly void ab initio and inoperative — it cannot be ratified even by a 100% unanimous vote of all shareholders
Valid if ratified later by an Ordinary Resolution of 51% shareholders
Valid as long as the venture earns a net profit above 15%
Binding on the company upon paying a ₹500 late fee to the bank

explanation: An act ultra vires (beyond the powers of) the MOA is null and void from the outset; not even unanimous shareholder consent can validate what the company lacked legal capacity to do, and directors become personally liable.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Documents Related to Formation of a Company

topic: Doctrine of Constructive Notice vs Indoor Management
questionText: How does the 'Doctrine of Indoor Management' (Turquand's Rule) protect honest outsiders dealing with a company against harshness of the 'Doctrine of Constructive Notice'?

options.text: It protects insiders/directors who forge signatures on share certificates
It abolishes public inspection of MOA and AOA at the ROC office

While outsiders are presumed to know the public MOA & AOA (Constructive Notice), they are entitled to assume in good faith that internal procedural resolutions required by the AOA have been properly complied with
It allows outsiders to enforce contracts that openly violate the MOA Object Clause

explanation: In Royal British Bank v. Turquand, courts held that once a transaction is consistent with registered MOA/AOA on its face, bona fide outsiders need not investigate internal boardroom regularities (subject to exceptions like forgery or actual knowledge of irregularity).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Documents Related to Formation of a Company

topic: Red Herring Prospectus vs Shelf Prospectus
questionText: Distinguish accurately between a 'Shelf Prospectus' (Section 31) and a 'Red Herring Prospectus' (Section 32):

options.text: A Shelf Prospectus omits the company's name and registered office

A Shelf Prospectus allows multiple securities issues over up to 1 year without filing a fresh prospectus each time (filing an Information Memorandum for updates), whereas a Red Herring Prospectus lacks complete particulars of exact price or quantum of securities during book-building
A Red Herring Prospectus is valid for 10 years, whereas a Shelf Prospectus is used only by Private Companies
Both prohibit listing on stock exchanges

explanation: Specified financial/public entities use a Shelf Prospectus (valid max 1 year) for repeated bond/security tranches; book-built IPOs file a Red Herring Prospectus at least 3 days before opening subscription to discover price.

questionText: In a Public Limited Company having share capital, how many subscribers must sign the 'Association (Subscription) Clause' of the MOA, and what minimum share commitment applies?

Only the Company Secretary signs without taking any share
At least 15 subscribers witnessed by a High Court Judge
At least 7 subscribers (2 for Private, 1 for OPC), each subscribing to at least 1 share in the presence of a witness

explanation: The Association Clause requires at least 7 subscribers for a Public Company (2 for Private, 1 for OPC), each writing opposite his/her name the number of shares taken (not less than one share), duly witnessed.

questionText: Maharashtra uniquely has TWO Registrars of Companies (ROC Mumbai and ROC Pune). If a company shifts its Registered Office from Nashik (under ROC Mumbai) to Kolhapur (under ROC Pune) WITHIN the same state of Maharashtra, whose approval is statutorily required besides a Special Resolution?

options.text: Prior Constitutional Amendment passed by Parliament
Approval of the Regional Director (RD) under Section 12(5)
Approval of the World Trade Organization
Only a Board Resolution — no shareholder vote or regulatory approval is needed

explanation: Changing the Registered Office from the jurisdiction of one ROC to another ROC within the SAME State (uniquely applicable in Maharashtra: Mumbai ↔ Pune, and Tamil Nadu: Chennai ↔ Coimbatore) requires a Special Resolution PLUS confirmation by the Regional Director!

topic: Ultra Vires the Directors/Articles vs Ultra Vires the Memorandum
questionText: The MOA of Sahyadri Power Ltd. empowers the company to borrow up to ₹100 crore, while its AOA restricts the Board of Directors to borrowing up to ₹25 crore without prior shareholder approval in General Meeting. If the Board borrows ₹40 crore without consulting shareholders, what is the legal position?

options.text: The borrowing is ultra vires the Directors/AOA (not ultra vires the MOA) — therefore shareholders CAN ratify it by altering/approving via resolution in General Meeting
The lender must forfeit the entire ₹40 crore to the state treasury
The borrowing is ultra vires the MOA and can never be ratified even unanimously
The borrowing is valid without any shareholder ratification because MOA overrides AOA automatically for directors

explanation: Crucial distinction: acts ultra vires the MOA are incurable, whereas acts within the MOA's ₹100 cr scope that merely exceed powers delegated to Directors/AOA can be ratified by shareholders!

topic: Civil and Criminal Liability for Misstatement in Prospectus
questionText: An IPO Prospectus falsely claims that the company owns patented lithium mines, inducing investors to subscribe; the claim turns out to be fabricated, causing subscriber losses. Under Sections 34 and 35 of the Companies Act, 2013, what liability arises?

options.text: Caveat Emptor ('buyer beware') shields directors completely from prospectus misstatements
Only the printing press owner is fined ₹1,000 while promoters keep all subscription money
Investors can claim compensation only after the company completes 25 years

Both criminal liability for fraud (under Section 34/447) AND personal civil liability (under Section 35) on directors, promoters, and experts who authorised the prospectus to compensate every aggrieved investor

explanation: Prospectus contracts are contracts uberrimae fidei (utmost good faith); untrue or misleading inclusions/omissions trigger severe criminal fraud punishment (Sec 34/447) and civil compensation liability (Sec 35) to harmed subscribers.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Documents Related to Formation of a Company

topic: Transfer vs Transmission of Shares
questionText: When title to shares passes automatically by 'operation of law' upon the death, insolvency, or lunacy of a member (without execution of a bilateral sale instrument or stamp duty), what is the process called?

options.text: Forfeiture of Shares
Buy-back of Shares
Transmission of Shares
Voluntary Transfer of Shares

explanation: Transfer of shares is a voluntary bilateral act between living parties for consideration, whereas Transmission occurs involuntarily by operation of law upon death (to legal heir/nominee), insolvency (to Official Receiver), or lunacy.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Members of a Company

topic: Subscribers to Memorandum Becoming Members
questionText: How do the Subscribers to the Memorandum of Association acquire membership in a newly incorporated company?

options.text: They never become members of the company
Only after purchasing shares from the secondary stock market two years later
Only if they are appointed Independent Directors
They are deemed to have agreed to become members automatically upon incorporation, and their names are entered in the Register of Members even without separate share application

explanation: Under Section 2(55)(i), subscribers to the MOA are statutory first members from the moment of company registration—neither formal application nor allotment letter is needed.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Members of a Company

topic: Register of Members
questionText: Aside from subscribers to the MOA and beneficial owners in depository (Demat) records, what two conditions are essential under Section 2(55) to become a 'Member' of a company?

options.text: Agreement in writing to become a member AND entry of the person's name in the company's Register of Members
Verbal promise to a broker AND holding a savings bank passbook
Attending a factory tour AND buying the company's retail products
Passing the ICSI exam AND residing at the registered office

explanation: Under Section 2(55)(ii), membership requires both a written agreement to become a member and actual registration of the person's name in the statutory Register of Members (MGT-1) (or beneficial-owner entry with a Depository for demat shares).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Members of a Company

topic: Partnership Firm Eligibility for Company Membership
questionText: Can a general Partnership Firm be registered in its own firm name as a Member in the Register of Members of a Joint Stock Company?

options.text: No — even individual partners are barred for life from buying shares
Yes — provided the firm has at least three sleeping partners
No — because a partnership firm is not a separate legal person (except if registering in a Section 8 charitable company); partners may, however, hold shares jointly in their individual names
Yes — every unregistered partnership firm is a corporate juristic person

explanation: Only legal persons competent to contract can be registered as members. Since a partnership firm lacks separate legal entity, it cannot hold shares in the firm's name (barring the special exception as member of a Section 8 company), though partners may register jointly.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Members of a Company

topic: Minor's Eligibility to Hold Shares
questionText: Under Indian Contract Act principles applied in Secretarial Practice, why do companies refuse allotment of PARTLY-PAID shares to a minor, yet permit registration of FULLY-PAID shares in the name of the minor's natural guardian?

options.text: Guardians are personally exempt from income tax on dividends
A minor's contract is void ab initio (Mohori Bibee rule) so future call money could never be legally enforced against a minor, whereas fully-paid shares carry zero future call liability
Fully-paid shares carry no dividend or capital value
Minors automatically hold 100% voting veto in General Meetings

explanation: Because a minor is incompetent to contract, a company cannot recover unpaid share calls from a minor; hence only fully-paid shares (no uncalled liability) may be held through a natural/legal guardian.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Members of a Company

topic: Cessation of Membership — Forfeiture vs Surrender
questionText: How does 'Forfeiture of Shares' differ from 'Surrender of Shares' as modes of cessation of membership?

options.text: Forfeiture is a compulsory penal cancellation initiated by the Board for non-payment of calls, whereas Surrender is a voluntary return of partly-paid shares by an unable member to avoid the formality of forfeiture (permitted only where forfeiture is justified and authorised by AOA)
Forfeiture gives the defaulting member double market price in cash, whereas Surrender doubles voting rights
Both apply exclusively to fully-paid equity shares
Surrender is ordered by customs authorities during export

explanation: Both extinguish membership on partly-paid shares (when authorised by AOA): Forfeiture is unilateral compulsory action by the Board after notice for call default; Surrender is voluntary hand-back as a shortcut to valid forfeiture.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Members of a Company

topic: Member Without Being a Shareholder vs Shareholder Without Being a Member
questionText: Give one legally valid example each of: (Case X) a person who is a 'Member' WITHOUT holding any shares, and (Case Y) a person who owns 'Shares' WITHOUT yet being a registered 'Member':

options.text: Case X: A bank manager granting overdraft; Case Y: An auditor signing the Balance Sheet
Case X and Case Y are legally impossible because Member and Shareholder are 100% identical in every case
Case X: A debenture-holder; Case Y: A trade creditor supplying raw materials

Case X: A member of a Company Limited by Guarantee having no share capital; Case Y: A transferee who has bought physical shares and holds a signed SH-4 transfer deed before the company registers the transfer

explanation: In Guarantee/Unlimited companies without share capital, members exist without shares (also a transferor remains a 'member' on the Register until the buyer's name replaces his); conversely, an unregistered transferee (or legal heir before transmission) owns beneficial share title before becoming a registered Member.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Members of a Company

topic: Membership by Estoppel / Acquiescence
questionText: Rohan never applied for shares in Zenith Ltd., yet his name was erroneously entered in the Register of Members; knowing this, Rohan attended an AGM and accepted a dividend warrant without protest. Six months later, Zenith Ltd. enters liquidation with ₹40 per share unpaid. Can Rohan now repudiate liability?

options.text: No — but his liability is capped at returning half the dividend only
No — under Membership by Acquiescence (Estoppel), having knowingly held himself out and enjoyed member privileges without getting the register rectified, he is liable as a contributory
Yes — absence of a written application form shields him even after cashing dividends
Yes — the Company Secretary personally pays Rohan's ₹40 call money

explanation: Under Section 2(55) / doctrine of holding out (Membership by Estoppel/Acquiescence), a person who knowingly permits his name to remain on the Register of Members and exercises membership rights cannot escape contributory liability when winding up supervenes.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Members of a Company

topic: Liability of Past Members (List B Contributories) vs Present Members
questionText: Meera transferred her partly-paid ₹100 shares (₹70 paid-up) to Kunal on 10th August 2025. If the company goes into winding up on 1st December 2025 (within 1 year of her ceasing to be a member) and Kunal defaults on the ₹30 uncalled balance, what are the statutory limits on Meera's liability?

options.text: Meera has unlimited personal liability for all post-August debts even if Kunal pays in full
Meera's liability vanished completely on 10th August 2025 the instant transfer was registered
Meera is liable up to ₹30 per share ONLY if Kunal fails to pay AND NOT for any corporate debts contracted AFTER 10th August 2025
Meera must pay ₹100 per share again regardless of ₹70 already paid

explanation: A past member (within 1 year prior to winding up) faces secondary liability capped strictly at unpaid face value (₹30), triggered only if present members cannot satisfy debts contracted BEFORE she ceased to be a member.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Members of a Company

chapter: Directors and Key Managerial Personnel of a Company
topic: Minimum and Maximum Number of Directors
questionText: Under Section 149(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, what is the statutory minimum number of Directors for an OPC, a Private Company, and a Public Company, and what is the normal maximum limit (without passing a Special Resolution)?

options.text: Minimum: 1 (OPC), 2 (Private), 3 (Public); Maximum: 15 Directors
Minimum: 1 (OPC), 3 (Private), 7 (Public); Maximum: 12 Directors
Minimum: 1 (OPC), 2 (Private), 5 (Public); Maximum: 50 Directors
Minimum: 2 (OPC), 5 (Private), 7 (Public); Maximum: 20 Directors

explanation: Section 149(1) mandates at least 1 director in an OPC, 2 in a Private Company, and 3 in a Public Company, with a cap of 15 directors—which a company may exceed by passing a Special Resolution.

chapter: Directors and Key Managerial Personnel of a Company
topic: Director Identification Number (DIN)
questionText: Before any individual can be appointed as a Director of a company under Section 152(3), what unique lifetime 8-digit number allotted by the Central Government must he/she hold?

options.text: Legal Entity Identifier (LEI)
Director Identification Number (DIN)
Importer Exporter Code (IEC)
Goods and Services Tax Network ID

explanation: Allotted under Sections 153–154, DIN is a unique person-specific identification number mandatory for anyone appointed as a company director; holding more than one DIN is prohibited under Section 155.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Directors and Key Managerial Personnel of a Company

chapter: Directors and Key Managerial Personnel of a Company
